title: Panic attack: an alarm from inside the body
description: A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear with strong bodily sensations, often with no outside danger. The episode follows the kind of attack that can be studied: one set off in a scanner by breathing air with extra carbon dioxide, which gives a feeling of not getting enough air, in someone with panic disorder. Very little about panic is settled, and only three regions are drawn changing; the third, the hypothalamus, rests on animal work. There is no "typical response" to compare with: the one study that compared groups reported a single difference, described in the brainstem text.
caveat: Spontaneous panic attacks are almost never caught in a scanner, so this episode is built from responses to carbon dioxide in the scanner, from reviews of scans of people with panic disorder doing other tasks, from a classic model based on fear learning in animals, and from one study of healthy volunteers being chased by a virtual predator. These were never one experiment. The role of the amygdala is unresolved: the classic model puts it at the centre, later reviews find it less consistently than predicted, and three people with no working amygdala had panic attacks when given carbon dioxide, more readily than other people, which suggests the amygdala may normally hold panic back. The brainstem is drawn as a rough outline of the whole structure because the small nuclei thought to be involved are not in the brain model. How an attack subsides has not been studied in scans.

phases.name: A signal from the body
phases.caption: It starts inside the body: here, carbon dioxide building up in the blood. In one study the brainstem, which monitors breathing, responded more strongly in people with panic disorder than in others.

phases.name: Alarm
phases.caption: The sensation is felt. The front of the insula, which carries the felt state of the body, becomes more active the worse the breathing feels; this was true of everyone studied, with or without panic disorder. Reviews also find the cingulate cortex behaving differently in panic disorder, without settling on how.

order.rationale: The breathing study averaged over two minutes of carbon dioxide and did not time the regions against each other. That the brainstem signal comes before the felt alarm is an inference from the body signal being the trigger.

phases.name: Peak
phases.caption: The height of the fear. In healthy volunteers facing a threat that closes in, activity shifts towards the midbrain, part of the brainstem; whether the same happens in panic is not known. In animals, the hypothalamus and brainstem drive the racing heart and fast breathing of fear.

order.rationale: The shift towards the midbrain was measured in healthy volunteers as a virtual predator approached, not during panic. Using it for the peak of a panic attack is an analogy.

phases.name: Subsiding
phases.caption: The attack passes. What the brain does as it subsides has not been studied in scans; this last part is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read for this episode followed the end of a panic attack. The return to baseline is assumed.

regions.explanation: More active in people with panic disorder than in others when they breathe air with extra carbon dioxide, in one study read as an abstract. A review also lists the brainstem in the network that behaves differently in panic disorder. In healthy volunteers, a midbrain area inside the brainstem, the periaqueductal grey, becomes active as a threat closes in, more so the greater the dread; that is not a panic finding and the area is not drawn separately.

regions.explanation: Drawn at baseline, because the sources disagree on what it does. The classic model of panic puts the amygdala at the centre, by analogy with fear learning in animals, and says so as speculation. Later reviews find it less consistently than that model predicts. Three people with no working amygdala on either side had panic attacks when given carbon dioxide, and did so more readily than other people, which the authors take to suggest that the amygdala may normally hold panic back.

regions.explanation: Evidence mainly from animals: there, signals reaching the hypothalamus and brainstem produce the bodily signs of fear, such as a racing heart. That the same happens in a human panic attack is the classic model's speculation, and nothing read for this episode measured it in people.
